text: Welcome to Speaking Club.
I'm Maya.
Let's open the memory box.
A drawing. Maybe a rainy afternoon and a box of crayons.
A ball. Perhaps a quick game of tag at recess.
A note. “Meet me at the park after school.”
A small toy. Maybe it had adventures across the rug.
Not every memory feels warm, and that's okay.
Today, you choose what to share. You can always pass.
So, what can an ordinary object remind us of?
Let's warm up with four questions.
Use the cycle: think, answer, give a reason, listen, and ask.
A fictional answer or a pass is always fine.
What games or activities did you enjoy when you were younger?
I used to play hide-and-seek on my street. We played until the streetlights came on.
Who did you usually play with?
Mostly the kids next door. Sometimes my cousin joined us.
What did you use to do after school or during your free time?
I used to ride my bike to the library. I loved the quiet and the comic books.
How often did you go?
Almost every Friday. It was my weekly adventure.
What is something you liked as a child but feel differently about now?
I loved spinning in circles on the playground. Now it makes me dizzy!
What made it so much fun?
The feeling of flying. I'd laugh until I fell over.
What do you think has changed most about childhood?
Many children have more screens now, but they still invent games. Some things stay the same.
What do you mean by 'invent games'?
Like rules for a game with just a ball and a wall.
Five useful words. Watch a short scene, then use each one.
Word banks are always one click away.
childhood. It means: the period of someone's life when they are a child.
For example: “Their childhood was very different from ours.”
I think the first one. When I was seven, I learned to ride a bike.
Many people think of games, school, and growing up.
imagination. It means: the ability to form ideas or pictures in your mind.
For example: “We used our imagination to turn the yard into a spaceship.”
I think the first one. A child turns a cardboard box into a castle.
I use it when I plan a surprise or imagine a new route home.
independent. It means: able to do things or make some decisions without help.
For example: “I became more independent when I learned to prepare a simple snack.”
I think the first one. Sam makes a sandwich without help.
Now I can cook dinner by myself without a recipe.
grow up. It means: develop from being a child into being an adult.
For example: “She grew up in a small town.”
I think the first one. Where did you grow up?
I grew up in a small town near a river.
look back on. It means: think about something from the past.
For example: “When he looks back on school, he remembers his art teacher.”
I think the first one. The past
I look back on my first art class with a smile.
Use the past simple for one event.
Use used to for old routines and states.
Careful: used to, be used to, and get used to have different meanings.
To tell a story: at first, then, after that, in the end.
At first, I used to be nervous on stage. Then I joined a drama club. In the end, I loved it.
I might use playground and take turns. We took turns on the playground swings.
Three short situations, all fictional.
There is more than one good answer. Give a reason.
A game feels fair when everyone knows the rules and gets a turn.
At recess, two teams are playing a ball game.
A new child walks over with a backpack.
The players say, “Sorry, our teams are full.”
Nobody wants to stop the exciting game.
I'd say, “Join us this round. We'll even out the teams.” That includes them without stopping the game.
Another idea: add a third team. Then nobody waits.
One more detail: the newcomer just moved here.
They don't know the rules yet.
If they don't know the rules, I'd explain the game in one minute, then invite them in.
My final answer: make space, explain simply, and keep playing.
Two friends borrowed a model bridge for a school project.
While carrying it, they dropped it. A small piece broke.
One friend whispers, “Let's hide it.”
The other says, “We should explain.”
I'd say, “I'm sorry. It broke when we dropped it. We'd like to fix it.” That's honest.
Yes, but I'd tell them first, then offer to repair it together.
One more detail: the owner arrives.
They ask, “Is everything okay with the bridge?”
With the owner right there, I'd answer honestly now. Waiting makes it harder.
My final answer: say what happened, apologize, and offer to help repair it.
A group has limited time to prepare a school event.
Some want a sports activity.
Others want an art activity.
And one person feels ignored.
I'd ask everyone for one idea, starting with the quiet person. Then we choose together.
I'd suggest a relay that mixes art and sports, so both groups can enjoy it.
One more detail: only thirty minutes are left.
And there is only one table.
With thirty minutes, I'd pick one simple activity and give everyone a role.
My final answer: hear every idea, then choose a simple plan that includes everyone.
Four claims. They are opinions, not facts.
Choose a place on the scale, then explain.
It depends. A plan helps me relax, but sometimes I want a free day.
Children need more free play than organized activities.
I partly agree. Free play builds creativity. But a good class can also teach teamwork.
How might age or circumstances change your answer?
For younger children, I'd say the answer changes. Older children can manage more.
I see your point, but I think the context matters.
Having chores helps children become more independent.
It depends. Small tasks can build confidence, but too many chores may be stressful.
Childhood friendships can be just as important as friendships made later.
I partly agree. One example would be a friend who knew you in difficult times.
Technology gives children more opportunities to be creative.
In some situations, yes. A child can make music or a short film. But paper and tape are creative too.
The second claim made me think. In some situations, chores help, but too many can be stressful.
You're planning a fictional childhood activity program.
All four qualities matter. This is a negotiation, not a judgment.
I'd pick cooperation. Children learn that a good idea is stronger when people build it together.
I would prioritize friendship. This matters because children join in when they feel welcome.
I would put independence first. This matters because children learn to try things on their own.
I see your point about friendship, but I'd put independence higher. Could we compromise by choosing both?
Could we compromise by choosing friendship and cooperation?
That works. Friendship and cooperation are our top two.
New situation: the group has mixed interests and only thirty minutes.
Should your priorities, or your planned activities, change?
With thirty minutes, I'd keep cooperation. Could we compromise by making two short stations?
Our top two stay the same, and our compromise is two short stations.
Time for a guessing game!
I hid one object in the memory box. Ask questions to find it.
Clue one: it was small and made of metal.
Clue two: I used to ring it every day on my way to school.
Was it a toy?
No, it wasn't. But it made a sound.
Was it a bicycle bell?
Yes! Well done!
It was a bicycle bell! Did you guess?
My mystery object used to be on my desk. It was long and yellow.
Was it a pencil?
Yes! One day, I lost it for a week. Did you use to lose pencils?
All the time!
Bonus challenge!
Use used to once, and add the words: one day.
My object used to hang by my bed. It was blue. One day, it stopped working.
Could you read with it?
Yes, I could. I used to read under the blanket.
Was it a flashlight?
Right! You're good at this.
The question about where I kept it helped most. It gave a picture in my mind.
Let's invent one story together.
Draw cards: a hero, a place, a problem, and an ending.
Take turns. Add one sentence each.
First, draw the hero and the place.
At first, a clever best friend sat alone at an old playground.
Then she noticed a small door under the slide.
After that, she called her friends to look.
Now, draw the problem!
Suddenly, the lights went out.
Then everyone held hands and moved slowly.
After that, they heard a quiet knock behind the door.
Last card: how does it end?
At last, a tiny robot opened the door from the other side.
In the end, a surprising friendship began.
At first, a clever best friend sat alone at an old playground. Then she found a small door under the slide.
After that, the lights went out, but a tiny robot opened the door. In the end, a surprising friendship began.
Would you rather read a book or watch a movie?
I'd rather watch a movie. There is no wrong answer.
Pass is always fine. A fictional choice is fine, too.
I'd rather draw. It feels quiet and calm.
Would you rather play your favorite childhood game again or watch your favorite childhood show again?
I'd rather play the game again. I'd love to move and laugh with other people.
What game would you play?
Hide-and-seek. It's simple and exciting.
Twist: You can only enjoy it for one hour.
With one hour, I'd still pick the game, but I'd choose a shorter one.
Would you rather invent a new playground game or design a new board game?
I'd rather invent a playground game. Movement and a few simple rules.
How would you explain it?
By showing it once. Pictures help, too.
Twist: Children in another country will play it, and you can't use spoken instructions.
With no spoken instructions, I'd pick the board game. Pictures on the cards would explain it.
Would you rather revisit a childhood place as it was then or see how it has changed today?
I'd rather see it as it was then. I'd like to remember the details.
What would you look for first?
The colors. I'd compare them with my memory.
Twist: You can look, but you can't touch or change anything.
If I can only look, I'd still choose the old place. Looking is enough.
Would you rather keep one meaningful childhood object or preserve one childhood story in a book?
I'd rather preserve a story. A story can be shared more easily.
Which story would you choose?
A story about a long walk home.
Twist: Someone you've never met will find it.
If a stranger finds it, I'd choose the story. It speaks for itself.
Would you rather have a treehouse or a secret clubhouse?
I'd rather have a treehouse, because I'd see the whole neighborhood.
Last task: a thirty-second story, real or fictional.
Use a routine or event, two expressions, and a clear ending. Then ask a question.
When I look back on my summers, I remember the lake. At first, I used to be afraid to swim.
Then a neighbor taught me to float. In the end, I swam across the lake!
How old were you when you swam across?
After school, I used to get along with the kids next door. We made up a game with a rope.
In the end, we took turns being the judge.
What were the rules?
I want to reuse “look back on.” It sounds natural when I talk about my past.
Keep speaking. Keep growing.
childhood
Their childhood was very different from ours.
imagination
We used our imagination to turn the yard into a spaceship.
independent
I became more independent when I learned to prepare a simple snack.
grow up
She grew up in a small town.
look back on
When he looks back on school, he remembers his art teacher.
One afternoon, we built a kite.
I used to play outside.
I used to be shy.
Did you use to...?
I didn't use to...
We used to walk to school.
I'm used to waking up early.
I got used to the new school.
During summer vacations, we would play cards after lunch.
I'd say, Join us this round. We'll even out the teams. That includes them without stopping the game.
I'd say, I'm sorry. It broke when we dropped it. We'd like to fix it. That's honest.
I would prioritize friendship first. This matters because children join in when they feel welcome.
I'd rather watch a movie.

Wonderful! Thank you for sharing.
Nice work! Every sentence counts.
That was brave. Well done!
